articles.title_orig: Death toll hits 31 after Russian strikes on a Ukrainian aid site, with dozens still missing
articles.title_zh: Death toll hits 31 after Russian strikes on a Ukrainian aid site, with dozens still missing
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of people were killed when Russia dropped at least nine bombs on a school building in southeastern Ukraine where they had taken shelter, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, describing it as “one of the deadliest attacks of this war.”
At least 33 people have been confirmed dead and another 50 are still unaccounted for after the attack on the building in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region, which local governor Mykhailo Semikin said was being used as a shelter and a humanitarian aid distribution center.
Semikin said they were in a newly-built, EU-funded reinforced basement designed to withstand most strikes, but the massive force of the bombs caused the concrete structure to collapse and a fire broke out.
The shelter was built last year in an effort to keep classes going during wartime, but many civilians have since left as the fighting got closer to the village, and it is not currently used as a school. Instead, local authorities are using it as an administrative center and humanitarian hub.
Masha’s husband was fighting on the front line. But she was the one killed by a Russian drone
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine highlighted in a statement on Tuesday that the attack took place just as civilians from the area gathered to receive humanitarian aid.
“The timing and location of the humanitarian distribution was well publicized,” said Danielle Bell, the head of the mission.
“Either the Russian armed forces knew that there was a humanitarian distribution taking place, or they failed to take the most basic steps to find out what was happening in this village they were planning to attack. In either case, this attack seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law.”
Zelensky said the attack came just before Russia launched another massive barrage of hundreds of drones and dozens of powerful cruise and ballistic missiles targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure – despite US President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for energy ceasefire .
“It is very telling that all of this is happening on the day of the US congressional elections. The Russians believe that America will not notice this signal from them. But such terror must be noticed and stopped,” Zelensky said on Tuesday morning.
“Ukraine must be helped to defend its skies, otherwise Russia will never stop its missile strikes. It is essential to help build peace honestly and reliably, and America can do that,” Zelensky added.
The latest attacks by Russia come amid a renewed push for negotiations by the Trump administration. US envoy Steve Witkoff recently held a meeting with Zelensky in Norway before flying to St. Petersburg to meet with the Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Separately, first lady Melania Trump helped to secure a ceasefire in the occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which enabled the evacuation of hundreds of civilians over the weekend. Trump’s office announced on Tuesday that the first lady would bring together representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, calling it “an extraordinary moment in American history.”
A Russian bomb attack killed at least 33 people in a Ukrainian village close to the frontline in the Zaporizhzhia region yesterday. CNN’s Clare Sebastian reports.
The strike on Monday is among the deadliest since the start of the war, but the past few months have been exceptionally bloody for Ukrainian civilians.
Russia ramped up its aerial attacks on towns and cities across the country over the summer, striking at all times of the day.
At least 33 people were killed last month when Russia hit two civilian buses in Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region. In August, 38 people were killed when a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot near the capital triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted hours in a residential area near Kyiv. And a mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage.
The assault against Komyshuvakha on Monday followed a familiar scenario in which Russian forces launch the first wave of strikes, wait for emergency services to arrive and then strike again.
At least two first responders, named locally as Denys Konovalenko and Oleksiy Sushchevsky, both 44, were killed after rushing to the scene of the first strike.
The Ukrainian Police said at least four of its officers have also been killed in the attack. They were named as Mykhailo Buzhenko and Mykola Balanda, both of who had more than two decades of police service under their belts, and Mykhailo Romanov and Dmytro Besedin, both of whom have been community police officers for more than a decade.
“(They) were helping local residents take shelter in an underground school. A treacherous follow-up strike trapped everyone who was trying to escape,” the police said in a statement.
Semikin told Ukraine’s national TV broadcast on Tuesday that Russia used KAB-500 and FAB-3000 bombs in the attack.
“To put this into perspective, this is a three-ton aerial bomb containing nearly 1.5 tons of explosive material; such weapons are primarily designed to destroy heavy concrete fortifications and bunkers,” he said.
CNN’s Kit Maher and Clare Sebastian contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.2 arrived last week with a variety of new features and changes for iPhone. Here are two new iOS 27.2 features I’ve been loving lately.
I’ve used Apple Podcasts for the last few years after previously sticking with third-party apps. The native Podcasts app won me over with excellent features like transcripts and automatic chapters .
My main hesitation in recommending the Podcasts app, however, has been its confusing Up Next queue. Thankfully, iOS 27.2 delivers a long-awaited fix.
In iOS 27.2, the Home tab in Apple Podcasts splits Up Next into two separate sections: New Episodes and Continue Playing.
These new sections offer, in my view, a much better system than what was there before. I no longer lose track of episodes I’ve previously started, since they’re not getting replaced by new episodes in my queue. Instead, there’s a clear divide between what’s new and what’s in-progress.
Shared Albums have long been one of my favorite features in Apple Photos. I don’t post on social media often, but I do love sharing photos and videos with close family and friends via the Photos app.
iOS 27 brought big upgrades to Shared Albums , the first notable changes in years. And to my surprise, Apple has already introduced even more improvements with iOS 27.2. Per Apple :
Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos
Support for editing captions and comments is long overdue, but a welcome addition. I also love the prompt that helps prevent duplicate photos, because I always find myself needing to double-check if I’ve shared certain photos already—now I don’t have to anymore.

articles.title_orig: China’s 22-Year Mangrove Restoration Drives Dramatic Rise in Coastal Bird Diversity
articles.title_zh: China’s 22-Year Mangrove Restoration Drives Dramatic Rise in Coastal Bird Diversity
articles.content_orig:
China has spent a quarter-century restoring its mangroves. A new study suggests the birds noticed.
Reporting in The Innovation , researchers at Ningbo University find that China’s mangrove area grew 166% between 1998 and 2020, from 10,617 to 28,194 hectares. Over the same 22 years, the number of bird species recorded along the coast rose from 148 to 397, and IUCN Red List threatened species from 11 to 21—a 91% rise.
The turnaround carries policy fingerprints: the 2000 China Wetland Protection Action Plan and the 2009 revision of the Marine Environmental Protection Law preceded the fastest growth phase, 2003 to 2008. Guangdong, Hong Kong, Macao, and Guangxi supplied 88% of the national increase, and average vegetation cover climbed from 31% to 38%—quantity and quality rising together.
The harder question is whether such restoration restores ecosystem function, not just tree cover. Birds make a practical yardstick: they sit high in the food web, respond quickly to habitat quality and food supply, and are counted by legions of volunteers. The team paired long-term satellite records of mangrove extent and density with those coastal bird observations, then used a path model to trace how mangroves might reach birds.
That model describes a chain: policy and a warming climate expanded mangrove area; larger, denser forests improved marine conditions and reshaped phytoplankton communities; bird diversity rose in step. Mangrove area tracked both bird abundance and richness closely (R² = 0.70–0.76, p < 0.001). Phytoplankton showed the strongest direct effect on overall diversity and abundance, and mangrove area the strongest on species richness. Climate had no significant direct effect—only an indirect one, through mangrove growth.
The authors are explicit about limits. Bird records come largely from observation databases in which survey effort varies by place and year, so part of the rise may reflect more observers rather than more birds. And denser mangrove is not uniformly good news: shorebirds that feed on open mudflats, such as sandpipers and plovers, can lose foraging ground when forest spreads across tidal flats. Restoration, the authors argue, should aim at a whole coastal wetland—mudflat, shallow water, and forest edge—not simply more trees.
Its contribution is scale and mechanism: a national, 22-year accounting that links a specific policy to a high-trophic-level group through measured environmental pathways, rather than a single correlation. The authors see the approach as transferable to other coastal nations weighing restoration against conservation commitments.

articles.title_orig: US Job Openings Jump to Four-Month High, Layoffs Decline
articles.title_zh: US Job Openings Jump to Four-Month High, Layoffs Decline
articles.content_orig:
Job openings surged in September, as did the number of workers who quit their positions, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday,while hiring also rose and layoffs dropped.
In its monthly look at labor market slack and worker mobility, the BLS reported job openings at 7.52 million, up 333,000 from August and well above the Dow Jones consensus outlook for 7.15 million.
As a share of the total workforce, the rate of job openings increased to 4.5%, up 0.2 percentage point from the prior month, according to the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey . There are now some 414,000 more job openings than workers classified as unemployed, or about 1.05 openings to every available worker.
Openings rose in manufacturing (54,000) as well as state and local government (108,000) and professional and business services (106,000).
At the same time, the total of employees leaving their jobs spiked to 3.36 million, an increase of 321,000 from August and the highest level since March 2025. Quits are considered a barometer for worker confidence in finding new jobs after leaving their prior positions.
"There are more job openings than unemployed people in the United States right now. That doesn't solve all problems, but it's a big change from a year ago," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "It's an encouraging sign that despite all the headwinds right now with high diesel and gas prices and ongoing inflation problems, companies are slowly increasing their hiring."
Hires rose on the month, up 131,000 to 5.4 million, while layoffs and discharges fell by 127,000 to 1.64 million, the lowest since March 2025.
The report comes ahead of the October nonfarm payrolls report, which the BLS will release Friday. The Wall Street consensus is for an increase of 59,000 after September eked out a gain of just 29,000, while the unemployment rate is figured to hold at 4.2%.
In other economic news Tuesday, September factory orders for manufactured goods jumped 1.8%, well above the estimate for 1.3% after increasing just 0.3% in August.

The powerful words from the King were careful and considered, and he spoke personally which will have landed with leaders - but he stopped short of a direct apology, our senior royal correspondent writes
The King also outlines what he describes as the "crisis of our time" , citing "brutal conflicts" facing the world, the "catastrophic reality" of climate change and the "dizzying speed" at which technology is transforming societies
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also at the summit, saying he is "open" to a formal apology from the UK over slavery, but said reparations were "not the right answer"
As part of talks with fellow leaders, Burnham is expected to set out plans for a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries dealing with the growing cost of paying interest
The Commonwealth leaders' summit is held every two years and allows leaders and representatives of the 56 nations to discuss the future of the partnership
Edited by Matt Spivey, with senior royal correspondent Daniela Relph and political editor Chris Mason in Antigua
Daniela Relph Senior royal correspondent, in Antigua
The King knew he couldn't give the audience exactly what they wanted today - which for many leaders would have been a straight apology for the transatlantic slave trade.
That will have disappointed many in the room but the King did speak with personal conviction and genuine sorrow.
These were the most extensive comments he has made on the UKâs role in the slave trade.
He was as candid as he could be in a role that a senior royal aide has described as "transcending politics" on this diplomatically delicate trip to the Caribbean
He is a constitutional monarch who is guided by the position of his government. That position may be shifting but for now it remains as no apology and no reparations.
The King was heard respectfully and warmly in the room by Commonwealth leaders and in the hours ahead we are likely to get reaction from them to the Kingâs words.
We're now bringing our live coverage to a close, you can read more in our news story.
Joe Coughlan Live reporter
The King met with various international representatives on Tuesday during his visit to Antigua and Barbuda
King Charles III today addressed Commonwealth leaders at a summit in which he called the slave trade the "most monstrous injustice" and a "shameful chapter" of history.
Speaking at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the monarch said the period "fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow" - but he did not offer a direct apology.
Britain's involvement in the transatlantic slave trade began in 1562, and by the 1730s it had become the world's biggest slave-trading nation. , external
The King spoke of the character and courage to overcome "monstrous injustice" to bring about an end to the international slave trade, in which he said the "the Royal Navy played such a leading role".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also attending the Chogm, which is held every two years, and is expected to set out plans for a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries. The summit continues tomorrow.
Before our coverage comes to a close, we will bring you some analysis of the King's speech from our senior royal correspondent Daniela Relph.
Successive prime ministers have ruled out making reparations for the UK's part in the transatlantic trade of enslaved people.
Last week Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was open "to calls for an apology" but called reparations "not the right answer".
He is expected to set out plans for a "debt reset".
This would aim to support Commonwealth countries dealing with the growing cost of interest on their debts. The Aids Health Foundation charity warned that one in three Commonwealth countries are in debt distress.
Alongside plans for a debt reset for these countries, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is also expected to allocate Â£40 million for infrastructure improvements in the Caribbean.
"Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting," the prime minister has said.
Bond, a network for organisations working in international development, welcomed the plan and said: "Too many Commonwealth countries are losing vital public revenue to unsustainable debt repayments and tax abuse, while struggling to fund their own public services including healthcare, education and climate resilience."
Protests, like this one in 2017, have called for the UK to make reparations for its involvement in the slave trade
King Charles referred to the slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" during his Commonwealth speech.
Buckingham Palace has been clear that it is not the King's role to decide whether the UK makes reparations for its part in the transatlantic trade of enslaved people.
Britain's involvement in the transatlantic slave trade began in 1562, and by the 1730s it had become the world's biggest slave-trading nation. , external
Between 1500 and 1800, around 12-15 million people were captured in Africa and taken to the Americas where they were forced to work as slaves. It is estimated that over two million people died on the journey.
The British Parliament passed more than one hundred acts supporting and protecting the slave trade and, with royal support and backing, had assisted the development of growing the enslaved African population in the British colonies.
British enslavers profited from the buying and selling of enslaved Africans to work on plantations and that trade became bound to Britain's economy and society.
Eventually, Parliament abolished the transatlantic slave trade in 1807, before banning enslaved labour colonies in 1833.
Daniela Relph Senior royal correspondent, in Antigua
The words, as ever from the King, were careful and considered. But he spoke personally and that will have landed in a room full of leaders - many of whom want more from the UK.
There was no direct apology or offer of reparations but there was a sense of sorrow and contrition from the King in his own words.
There was an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the brutality of the slave trade.
But there was also a sense from the King that the most powerful way forward is to look to the future and ensure the next generation of young people in the Commonwealth have the best opportunities made available to them.
âEvil need not have the last word,â the King said.

"Each of you has the opportunity to make the greatest possible difference, I pray that over the coming days you will embrace this opportunity and commit yourselves to action," he says.
Above all, he says he trusts that each of the gathered leaders will commit to a Commonwealth in which "our young people can look to the future with greater confidence and purpose".
He ends by saying that he hopes people can draw inspiration from "this remarkable family of nations" as he himself has "always done".

articles.title_orig: NATO’s New Defense Plan Would Mean Strikes Deep Inside Russia
articles.title_zh: NATO’s New Defense Plan Would Mean Strikes Deep Inside Russia
articles.content_orig:
Admiral Rob Bauer, former Chair of the NATO Military Committee, expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform on the sidelines of a special event organized by the Brussels office of the Kyiv Security Forum.
"Ukraine has to fight this war in a certain way because it was limited by the U.S. and other Western nations in the use of certain weapon systems or not allowed to use some of them. So NATO is not going to fight exactly the same way as Ukraine is fighting the Russians," Bauer said.
He explained that in the event of an attack, the Alliance would deploy its air force and navy and launch long-range precision strikes against Russian territory.
"This is something that Ukraine is now doing more and more with weapon systems that it has developed yourself. As you were limited at the outset, you started to work on the drones. So in a way, the drones were your answer to a limited amount of artillery ammo. The fact that you are successful in that area now is a testament to the fact that you found an answer to the fact that you were not supported as we should have supported you," the admiral said.
Even Ukraine's possession of a certain number of F-16 fighter jets cannot match the capabilities of a full fleet of strategic bombers, F-35s, F-22s, F-15s, F-16s and other assets available to the Alliance, Bauer said.
He added that the Alliance's regional plans are fully aligned with the tasks at hand.
"General Grynkewich, NATO's SACEUR, talked about this at a forum in Warsaw just a couple of weeks ago. His message was that Article 5 is ironclad and that the U.S forces in Europe will fight within NATO to first block the Russians, then blunt them if necessary, and if it takes longer, to break them. We are talking about the industrial complex and the logistics support of a longer war that we will have to break, as Ukraine is doing now with Russia, with its refineries and everything else," the admiral said.
Asked whether he believed all NATO allies would have the political will to repel an aggressor, Bauer said: "General Grynkewich would never have been able to say this in Warsaw if it hadn't been exclusively approved by the White House."
In Bauer's view, this was "a message from President Trump to NATO: America is with NATO, article 5 is ironclad, and the regional plans are in place."
He also explained that if intelligence indicated Russia was building up its forces and the Alliance knew which direction they might try to advance in, "the battle groups can be strengthened from 1,000 to 5,000, to a brigade size in different nations."
"At the political level, these plans have already been agreed, so at a certain stage, within those plans, certain things are going to happen," the admiral said.
He added that the situation had been different in the past, when many of these measures would have been debated, with questions raised about whether they were necessary.

Brent crude plunged more than $6 per barrel Tuesday morning, falling from $107.24 to $100.80 before recovering to around $104 shortly after 10 a.m. Eastern, as traders reacted to a succession of conflicting reports about U.S.-Iran peace negotiations.
The selloff followed Monday's 7.6% decline, which left Brent at $104.77. Prices initially rebounded overnight after reports of U.S. strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz, before reversing sharply Tuesday morning.
The first abrupt decline began moments before a Bloomberg-attributed breaking headline announcing that Iran's supreme leader had authorized negotiations on previously non-negotiable issues.
But that was a stronger claim than Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's statement that the supreme leader had only granted the government additional negotiating authority. Pezeshkian had not specified which issues might be discussed.
Questions subsequently emerged about whether the Bloomberg headline accurately reflected the Iranian statement.
Brent suffered another steep drop around 8:20 a.m, right around the time of an Al Jazeera report that Washington had approved a draft agreement presented through Qatari mediators.
Additional reports surfaced that Washington and Tehran had made concessions involving Iran's nuclear program and frozen assets, citing Al Araby Al Jadeed. The Al Araby report described a proposed exchange of Iranian nuclear concessions for the release of frozen funds.
But a senior Iranian official has rejected the claim that there was a breakthrough over concessions, and clarified that an agreement was indeed still far off. Tehran’s public position has been and still is that its conditions must be met before Hormuz can reopen, and nuclear negotiations can begin only after those are met.
In other words, nothing substantial has officially changed.
Qatar confirmed that both sides were reviewing proposals, and no agreement has been announced.
The competing reports help explain the uncertainty surrounding Tuesday's trading, although they do not establish what caused either sharp decline. Momentum trading and automated orders may have amplified the moves.
By midmorning, Brent had recovered nearly $3 from its session low. The reported diplomatic breakthroughs remain unverified, and the Strait of Hormuz remains restricted.
By Julianne Geiger for Oilprice.com

articles.title_zh: King Charles to Give ‘Unflinching’ Speech on UK’s Role in Slave Trade
articles.content_orig:
King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summit of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.
He said the trade in enslaved persons "still casts a shadow" over the association of nations.
There has been calls from some for the UK to make a formal apology for its historic role in the trave trade ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, but there was not one in the King's address.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is also at the summit, has previously said he is open to Britain issuing a formal apology but that financial reparations were "not the right answer".
While there was no direct apology, he did offer some contrition - and there was also an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the legacy of the slave trade.
He said: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth.
"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."
He told the summit: "The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."
King Charles continued: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know.
"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures – the good they did as well as the wrongs."
The King's address also referenced the "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, the "catastrophic reality" of climate and rapid technological development.
The Chogm meeting gathers leaders from 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth, a voluntary grouping made up primarily of former territories of the British Empire.
The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
The King and Queen are on a tour of the Caribbean which has reignited difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Micron (NASDAQ: MU) has had a fantastic year, with the stock up over 200%.
The memory maker became the center of the next major bottleneck in artificial intelligence. As clusters of graphics processing units (GPUs) scaled to meet the needs of larger AI models, memory, which feeds data to the GPUs in various capacities, also came into high demand.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Memory prices soared, resulting in fantastic results for companies like Micron. Here's what $6,000 invested in the stock could be worth by 2029.
Micron is one of the largest makers of NAND flash memory and dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), both of which play different roles in feeding data to GPUs .
NAND is cheaper and offers high-capacity storage useful for holding the massive data sets that feed GPUs during training.
DRAM is high-speed memory that holds data only while powered. In AI systems, stacks of DRAM silicon are used to create high bandwidth memory (HBM), which sits next to GPUs and holds model parameters during training and inference.
Due to the massive demand for AI and, therefore, GPUs and data, Micron COO Manish Bhatia said on the company's most recent earnings call that "we really don't have line of sight to when supply and demand balances."
Memory companies are often viewed as cyclical because it's difficult to match supply with demand, which can result in a supply glut at some point in the cycle. In this super-charged cycle, many investors have wondered if things will be different.
Micron has secured 16 Strategic Customer Agreements, with deals running three to five years, an atypical development for memory companies.
As a result of all this, Micron's earnings are projected to soar. Micron recently completed its fiscal year 2026 (ending Aug. 26), reporting diluted earnings per share of over $74. For fiscal year 2027, Wall Street consensus estimates project Micron's earnings to surge to over $172 per share, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence .
In fiscal 2029, the 10 Wall Street analysts who have submitted estimates to S&P Global expect Micron's earnings to exceed $212 per share. Valuing Micron on its current forward 12-month earnings of roughly $172, the stock trades at a 5.65x multiple.
If I simply carry that multiple forward, Micron should trade at $1,197 per share in 2028, based on its forward projected earnings for fiscal 2029. That implies roughly 23% upside, meaning a $6,000 investment would be worth $7,380.
Currently, the market largely still doesn't believe this cycle is different, which is why Micron, despite significantly higher earnings, trades at a mid-single-digit multiple.
Some on Wall Street believe the company deserves more credit. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria stated in a recent research note earlier this month that "investors are early in their journey of understanding Micron's value, and that journey will lead them to assigning a far higher multiple."
The growth in earnings has been staggering, given that Micron generated only $7.59 in diluted earnings per share in fiscal 2025. If it can maintain earnings in the high $100s or low $200s, then Luria is likely right and the stock will rerate.
A 10x forward earnings multiple would imply a $2,120 stock price based on the fiscal 2029 earnings estimate, suggesting more than double Micron's current price. In that case, a $6,000 investment would be worth roughly $12,940 in 2028.
Investors are right to be skeptical, because it's quite possible Micron and other memory makers are over-earning.
Recently, reports of a new memory chip from China that could fit more memory in a denser area spooked the market, as did reports from South Korea citing industry experts who believe heavy supply will enter the market in 2029.
So, it's tough to predict how sustainable Micron's earnings are. That's why I believe owning some Micron stock is fine right now, but investors won't want to go in too heavy on the stock, which could be very volatile, even long-term.

articles.title_orig: Mining giant joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia
articles.title_zh: Mining giant joins fight to stop killer toad march across Australia
articles.content_orig:
Rio Tinto is ploughing millions of dollars into stopping the poisonous cane toad reaching the Pilbara region of western Australia, where the mining giant has a vast iron ore operation.
The firm, alongside Curtin University in Perth and others, will spend A$28m (£14.5m) building a "toad containment zone" to prevent the pest travelling south.
While the cane toad is not a direct threat to Rio Tinto's business, it produces toxins lethal to native wildlife and poses a threat to Pilbara's ecosystem.
Rio Tinto has previously faced criticism for destroying two sacred Aboriginal rock shelters in Pilbara which sat above tonnes of iron ore.
The decision cost the former chief executive his job, provoked a widespread backlash and saw Rio Tinto commit to rebuilding trust with Indigenous communities.
Commenting on the proposed containment zone, Roberta Hunter, a ranger in Australia's Nyangumarta Warrarn Indigenous Protected Area, said: "Cane toads destroy the water and animals.
"When toads come close to our country, we want to be there to stop them because we don't want the country to be destroyed."
The plan is to cut off the toad's water supply by building a barrier across 7,500 sq km (2,895 sq m) of land between the Great Sandy Desert and the Indian Ocean.
In drier months, the cane toad needs water every few days to survive.
If there are no natural water sources, the toad relies on artificial water points normally used for cattle and irrigation.
The funding will be used to stop the toad accessing dams, storage tanks or other ground-level water sources. The five-year project will begin in 2027.
A number of native species are at risk if the toad gets into Pilbara. These include the northern quoll, whose numbers have been decreasing, the goanna lizard and the ghost bat.
The toads were introduced into Australia in 1935 to control beetles within the sugar cane industry.
Since then, they have been on a slow march west across the country's northern landscape, according to the Australian government, travelling between 40 km and 60 km a year.
There are no predators or diseases that control the toads, which defend themselves using poison.
Ben Phillips, a professor at Curtin University, said the toads would reach Pilbara within two decades without action.
He said: "The toad containment zone is a once in a lifetime opportunity to stop one of the world's worst invasive species in its tracks and protect the region's unique wildlife."

articles.title_orig: SpaceX and Musk Have Big Wireless Ambitions. Boost Mobile Won’t Fulfill Them.
articles.title_zh: SpaceX and Musk Have Big Wireless Ambitions. Boost Mobile Won’t Fulfill Them.
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SpaceX ( SPCX ) may be attempting an end run to circumvent obstacles it's facing in getting a mobile network off the ground.
Per the Washington Post , SpaceX is in talks with EchoStar ( SATS ) about launching its own wireless phone service through Boost Mobile, after the country's three biggest carriers — Verizon, AT&T ( T ), and T-Mobile ( TMUS ) — reportedly turned down SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Musk met with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen last month, according to two people familiar with the negotiations cited by the Post. The talks could end with SpaceX buying Boost Mobile outright or getting access to its network, which the discount carrier leases from AT&T and T-Mobile.
In recent months, Musk asked the heads of Verizon ( VZ ), AT&T and T-Mobile to let SpaceX use their networks for its own mobile service. All three said no, per the Post.
But there may be a catch to SpaceX's plan. Typically, a carrier's lease agreement can't be transferred to a new owner without the host carrier's permission, meaning AT&T and T-Mobile may still need to approve a Boost deal to provide access to SpaceX.
SpaceX is open about its ambitions in the terrestrial mobile space. On the company's recent earnings call , CFO Bret Johnsen said the goal is to "become a major mobile carrier ... in the United States." SpaceX also recently agreed to buy $8 billion worth of wireless spectrum licenses intended for cellular service in places satellites can't reach.
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said on X .
SpaceX and EchoStar already have a relationship. In September 2025, SpaceX agreed to buy EchoStar's AWS-4 and H-block spectrum licenses for about $17 billion, split between up to $8.5 billion in cash and up to $8.5 billion in SpaceX stock, EchoStar said at the time . SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said the deal would "advance our mission to end mobile dead zones."
What SpaceX still lacks is a ground network. Its satellite signal isn't strong enough yet to carry cell coverage indoors or in dense cities, where most phones are - and that's why a deal with Boost would be so crucial.
An MVNO (mobile virtual network operator) like Boost rents capacity on an existing carrier's network. Last month, TD Cowen's Gregory Williams called acquiring an MVNO the cheapest and fastest route for SpaceX to launch mobile service, noting a network build would cost "upwards of $80B" and take years.
The Big 3, he said, still show no desire "to (ever) sign an MVNO deal with Starlink that could ravage the industry."
Carrier executives have publicly doubted that SpaceX can rebuild their tower networks. Verizon's CEO put the build-out at four to six years. Musk said it would take about half that.
"Veterans of the cellular industry look at the chess board of existing pieces and don't see a solution," Musk said recently on X . "They don't understand that SpaceX is developing entirely new pieces that fundamentally alter the strategic landscape."

articles.title_zh: Bill Ackman warns of 'casino' stock market as speculative trading grows
articles.content_orig:
Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman ’s mega-cap tech holdings reflect his strict framework for long-term investing. Ackman holds Microsoft Corp. MSFT , Amazon.com Inc. AMZN , and Netflix Inc. NFLX in his portfolio, favoring the type of durable businesses that he says remain ‘enormously valuable’ over two decades.
In a podcast interview with Nicolai Tangen , CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management, Ackman defined his criteria for an ideal stock.
“A great company is a business you could buy today. The markets could shut for 20 years, and you know with an enormous degree of certainty that you’ll own something that’s enormously valuable 10 or 20 years from now,” Ackman said . He added that Pershing Square prefers “businesses that look like royalty collecting companies like annuities.”
Ackman applies this long-term framework to his technology holdings. During an interview on CNBC‘s “Squawk on the Street,” Ackman defended the heavy artificial intelligence capital expenditures by Amazon and Microsoft.
He described the tech giants as “well capitalized incredibly dominant franchises that have the balance sheets to make these investments.” Ackman stated that unlike smaller competitors, “ Microsoft and Amazon are going to and Meta will be able to use every incremental watt if you will of compute.” Speaking to Tangen, Ackman noted that those names “represent about a third of our portfolio today.”
Ackman also expressed conviction in Netflix during his CNBC appearance, referring to the company as a “high growth utility.”
He told CNBC that investors can “buy the stock today at one of the lowest valuations in history,” noting it was trading around 18 times earnings. Ackman stated that he expects Pershing Square’s internal rate of return on the stock to be “well north of, you know, well into the 20s,” projecting that earnings growth is going to be in the “mid to high teens for the foreseeable future.”

articles.title_orig: The 5 most brutal political moggings of 2026
articles.title_zh: The 5 most brutal political moggings of 2026
articles.content_orig:
The Collins English Dictionary announced its 2026 word of the year Tuesday morning, with judges opting for “mogging.”
For readers not fluent in youth culture: Mogging “might involve making [anyone] look inferior in terms of appearance, confidence or status — anything, really,” according to marketing consultant and copywriter Rachel Quin, who authored a Collins article announcing the winner.
According to Collins, the term originated in the bodybuilding community as a shortening of AMOG (“alpha male of the group”) and penetrated into the so-called manosphere , a collection of typically online male communities united by their beliefs about masculinity.
“Fast forward to 2026 and it’s everywhere,” Quin added. And, crucially for POLITICO’s purposes, it can be applied to literally any situation.
With that in mind, we looked back at five top political moggings in 2026 — the more brutal, the better.
One minute, Keir Starmer was British prime minister with a thumping Labour majority cheering his every move. The next, he was humiliated and ousted by a northern rival who had done little to hide his own leadership ambitions.
Starmer, of course, tried to block the Downing Street takeover by Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham.
But once Burnham loyalists and grumpy ministers had quit Starmer’s government in droves, the prime minister bowed out this summer after just two years in office and Burnham — having manufactured, at the second attempt, an opportunity to enter parliament — waltzed into the top job unopposed.
Call it the textbook framemog.
Mozambique’s towering president, Daniel Chapo — who stands more than two meters tall — loomed over tiny Russian leader Vladimir Putin at a summit between African countries and Russia in Moscow last week.
Countries signed a summit declaration pledging to expand “cooperation in energy, minerals, and digital technology, establishing Russian industrial zones in Africa, and localizing production” — but the defining image of the summit was a photo of Chapo dwarfing Putin .
Looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular, real name Braden Peters, likely breathed a sigh of relief, having suffered the year’s other most notorious framemogging, at the hands of internet character ”ASU frat leader.”
In a classic case of nominative determinism, Jacob Rees-Mogg, former British government minister and current haunted pencil, pantsed American commentator Tucker Carlson in a discussion on the latter’s YouTube channel in October.
Rees-Mogg may not have expected to find himself defending Britain’s decision to fight against Adolf Hitler, but that’s what happened after Carlson questioned why Britain had even bothered entering World War II against Nazi Germany.
Rees-Mogg said he was very surprised that Carlson was “verging on defending Hitler,” adding: “I think this is not really what you want to be doing,” in a clip that went viral and catapulted the Brexit hard-liner back into the British public consciousness.
Donald Trump’s bid to clean out the iconic Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C. was initially hampered by persistent pond scum.
After a money-spinning renovation in early summer, algae came back with a vengeance, turning the water green and murky, while the blue paint job began to peel off the pool bottom.
Rather than turn his ire toward the contractors, Trump blamed vandals for attacking the pool, and his Department of Justice attempted to prosecute people it accused of damaging the site. Judges, however, dropped or dismissed the criminal cases.
Trump returned to the theme Monday — right before America went to the polls for midterm elections in which the country is laser-focused on the surging cost of living and corruption — holding a rally in front of the pool and recounting all the issues he said he’d fixed with the pool, including “tremendous algae.”
In Hungary’s biggest aura battle ever , conservative challenger Péter Magyar defeated longtime nationalist leader Viktor Orbán, ending 16 years in power for the populist prime minister.
Magyar, a former MP for Orbán’s Fidesz party, dramatically broke ranks in 2024, releasing a tape of his ex-wife apparently incriminating members of Orbán’s inner circle in a corruption scandal when she was justice minister. For two years, he consistently attacked Fidesz and Orbán over graft while building a movement to take down the EU’s problem child.
Magyar ultimately led a big-tent campaign focusing on cost-of-living concerns and pro-EU messaging, which turned into a landslide election victory that left Trump and the Kremlin salty .

There’s a lot of mystery around the finances of major AI labs, and as Anthropic inches towards its IPO, we’re starting to get some answers. In particular, the company is finally disclosing more about the economics of compute, and how much it of Anthropic’s skyrocketing revenue is being lost to compute costs.
In a new filing on Monday , Anthropic released data that showed those margins on compute actually getting worse. The filing was an update to the S-1 released last week — but where that filing’s financial disclosures only covered through June 30th of this year, the new data extended to disclose results through an extra quarter, to September 30th. Broadly, Anthropic had a good quarter: revenue reached $17 billion, up from $11.5 billion in the previous quarter, suggesting durable growth. But the operating loss grew at the same time, thanks in large part to growing compute costs.
Looking at the compute margins makes the picture even worse. In the new quarter, compute took up 58% of the company’s revenue, up from 48% the quarter before. At a moment when the company could win over IPO investors by showing margins improving, they’re getting worse.
A chart in the filing shows this even more clearly, tracking the company’s revenue for every dollar spent on compute. Since the start of 2025, it’s been steadily growing, peaking at just over 2x this past quarter, then falling back down to 1.72x
Many indications imply that this shift in compute margins is more of a blip than a long-term problem, but it still tells us important things about the business of running a major lab. Trying to keep up with demand, Anthropic’s compute bill shot up to $10 billion for the quarter, including, as the filing notes, “$5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments.” Basically, demand was growing so fast that Anthropic had to scramble for compute, which meant paying higher rates.
Some of those deals have already played out in public. Anthropic has been paying SpaceX $1.25 billion a month for compute, alongside multi-billion dollar deals with Nscale , Akamai and Volta . In the parlance of the industry, these are neoclouds rather than hyperscalers — smaller outfits that offer more flexible compute deals at higher rates.
Anthropic’s margins got worse in Q3 because of deals like these, and there’s no sign they’ll be able to do without them anytime soon. As the new filing puts it, “We expect compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain our largest operating expense for the foreseeable future as additional committed compute becomes available to us under multi-year arrangements with CSPs, and as we continue to invest in additional compute.”
Anthropic is still trying to lower its compute costs. In particular, the company talks quite a bit about its efforts to build its own compute base under a project it calls “Anthropic Direct.” But with demand growing so fast, those efforts aren’t going to be able to keep pace, and the neoclouds will continue to be the best option they have.
In a sense, these are champagne problems. As long as revenue is growing at nearly 50% a quarter, few investors will worry about high compute costs — and the moment demand slows down, investors may be comforted by a compute picture that has gotten a lot sunnier. But it’s a reminder of how much AI labs still depend on the trillion-dollar infrastructure buildout — and how vulnerable they are to hiccups in that process. It’s easy to imagine the data center buildout slowing down over the next year if bond markets get skittish or local opposition gets more intense. There’s not much Anthropic can do to address either of those risks, and either one would make a messy compute picture a whole lot messier.
In the meantime, the future of Anthropic and other labs will be at the mercy of compute prices.

articles.content_orig:

In less than four years, the MTA could be looking at a nearly $900 million funding shortfall as spending outpaces fare revenue, according to a new analysis from the Citizens Budget Commission, which recommends cutting the workforce to close the gap.
The budget watchdog recommends sweeping job cuts to positions that it argues technology has made obsolete. The budget commission suggested the MTA allow its trains to run with just one worker, instead of two.
Train lines that have new computer-based signals, like the L and the 7, are already fully automated, as are the announcements on the trains. While the conductor opens and closes the train doors, the operator has few other duties, which include hitting a button every 20 seconds to signal they are alert. The budget commission cited the operator’s limited responsibilities as a sign the job could be cut with no impact to service.
Eliminating operator jobs on the L and 7 lines could save $36.5 million a year, according to the report . If the agency moved to phase out two people operating trains across the system, it could save $500 million a year.
The agency is in the process of installing new signals on other lines like the A, C, E, F, G, M and R lines. For now, those lines still require two people to run the trains.
The suggestion from the Citizens Budget Commission comes at a sensitive time as Transport Workers Union Local 100 negotiates a contract with the MTA for its 40,000 subway and bus workers. The MTA is expected to release its financial plan for next year in the coming weeks, which will include a 4% fare and toll increase. The board will vote on that plan in December.
“The same recommendations have been coming down for dozens of years, so there's nothing new about it,” said Transport Workers Union of America President John Samuelsen. “It's essentially a recommendation to balance alleged deficits that the MTA has off the backs of working people.”
Last year, the state legislature tried to enshrine a requirement of two MTA workers on each train into law, but Gov. Kathy Hochul vetoed the bill , leaving open the possibility that one-person train operations could happen in the future.
“Legislatively mandated staffing prevents the MTA from modernizing — as technology and best practices continue to improve — and realizing the efficiency and financial benefits,” the Citizens Budget Commission's report argues.
The Citizens Budget Commission acknowledges the MTA has become more efficient in recent years, saving a reported $576 million this year through what the agency calls “operating efficiencies.” But the report argues that without cutting labor and healthcare costs, the MTA faces a $300 million budget gap next year that will grow to $900 million by 2030. The budget commission estimates its recommended reforms could save $2.5 billion annually.
Other recommendations include streamlining fare collection on the commuter railroads by checking tickets prior to boarding, reducing the need for someone to walk through the train. The Citizens Budget Commission argues cutting more than 1,000 jobs on Metro-North and the Long Island Rail Road could save $380 million annually.
The report also recommended MTA retirees pay more in healthcare premiums, which could bring in an additional $315 million a year.
Samuelsen countered that many laborers, ironworkers, track workers, and crane operators in the MTA get paid less than their peers in the private sector, but accept that because of the generous retirement benefits.
"The CBC is right to note that we've made extraordinary progress in securing hundreds of millions of dollars in new recurring operational efficiencies," MTA spokesperson Mitch Schwartz wrote in a statement. He did not address the proposal to eliminate jobs.

Since 2008 he has reported on everything from Occupy Wall Street, the rebuilding of the World Trade Center site, Hurricane Sandy, to Trump’s campaign for president. Shares of Shopify (NASDAQ: SHOP) were sharply lower on Tuesday, falling as much as 13.2%. As of 12:41 p.m. ET, the stock was still down 5.4%.
The catalyst that sent the e-commerce platform and tools provider lower was its financial results, which failed to instill investors with confidence.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Before the market open, Shopify reported its third-quarter results, but shareholders simply weren't inspired. The company reported revenue of $3.74 billion, up 32% year over year, which resulted in adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $0.49, up 44%.
To give the results context, analysts' consensus estimates called for revenue of $3.73 billion and adjusted EPS of $0.46 -- so Shopify cleared both hurdles with room to spare.
The strong top-line growth was fueled by a 29% increase in gross merchandise volume (GMV), or the total value of products sold on its platform. At the same time, monthly recurring revenue (MRR) of $230 million climbed 19%.
President Harley Finkelstein highlighted the company's strengths, saying, "Shopify is uncommonly good at operating in two realities at the same time: the world our merchants exist in today, and the one they are moving toward. Q3 is the perfect example. We powered $119 billion in GMV, while continuing to build commerce into every surface, every agent, and increasingly, everywhere."
For the upcoming fourth quarter, Shopify is guiding for revenue growth in the low-thirties percentage rate year over year, accompanied by gross profit in the high twenties and free cash flow margin similar to last year's rate of about 19%.
That all seems like positive news, so why is Shopify stock falling? Investors found nits to pick with some of the company's operating metrics. GMV of $119.2 billion fell short of the $120.1 billion analysts had predicted, while subscription revenue of $836 million was below the $850 million some expected.
At 99 times earnings, Shopify stock isn't cheap, so investors are more likely to nitpick its results. That said, the stock is valued at a significant discount to its three-year average multiple of 169.

articles.title_zh: Ukraine's Zelenskyy on defying US in attacking Russian oil: 'Our response must be painful'
articles.content_orig:
Drones attacked an oil refinery in Yaroslavl in Yaroslavl Oblast on the night of 2-3 November, causing a large fire at the facility.
Source: Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channels Exilenova+ , Exile+ and Supernova+ ; Russian media outlet Astra ; Yaroslavl Oblast Governor Mikhail Yevrayev
Quote from Astra: "The Slavneft-YANOS oil refinery (Slavneft-Yaroslavnefteorgsintez), also known as the Yaroslavl Oil Refinery, is one of Russia's five largest refineries.
Having examined photos and videos sent in by readers, an Astra OSINT expert determined that the facility on fire is indeed this refinery, located in the city of Yaroslavl."
Details: Photos and videos posted after the attack show a large fire breaking out on the refinery's premises.
An air-raid warning was issued at around 03:00 due to a drone threat in the area, followed later by a missile alert.
Slavneft, which owns the Yaroslavl refinery, is jointly controlled by Rosneft and Gazprom Neft. The plant produces petrol, diesel fuel, fuel oil, aviation kerosene, lubricants, paraffin and other petroleum products.
The facility also supplies petroleum products to Russia's Central and Northwestern Federal Districts and provides fuel to Moscow Oblast.
The refinery's customers also include facilities belonging to Russia's defence industry. For example, the plant supplies fuel for Russian military aircraft and equipment.
Background: The Yaroslavl refinery has been attacked several times before. In particular, the plant was targeted by Ukraine's defence forces in late September.

articles.title_zh: 5 iPhone Features You Should Be Using After Updating To iOS 27
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.2 arrived last week with a variety of new features and changes for iPhone. Here are two new iOS 27.2 features I’ve been loving lately.
I’ve used Apple Podcasts for the last few years after previously sticking with third-party apps. The native Podcasts app won me over with excellent features like transcripts and automatic chapters .
My main hesitation in recommending the Podcasts app, however, has been its confusing Up Next queue. Thankfully, iOS 27.2 delivers a long-awaited fix.
In iOS 27.2, the Home tab in Apple Podcasts splits Up Next into two separate sections: New Episodes and Continue Playing.
These new sections offer, in my view, a much better system than what was there before. I no longer lose track of episodes I’ve previously started, since they’re not getting replaced by new episodes in my queue. Instead, there’s a clear divide between what’s new and what’s in-progress.
Shared Albums have long been one of my favorite features in Apple Photos. I don’t post on social media often, but I do love sharing photos and videos with close family and friends via the Photos app.
iOS 27 brought big upgrades to Shared Albums , the first notable changes in years. And to my surprise, Apple has already introduced even more improvements with iOS 27.2. Per Apple :
Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos
Support for editing captions and comments is long overdue, but a welcome addition. I also love the prompt that helps prevent duplicate photos, because I always find myself needing to double-check if I’ve shared certain photos already—now I don’t have to anymore.
There are a ton of other great additions in iOS 27.2, which you can read about below:

articles.title_orig: Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia
articles.title_zh: Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Fishermen stand on the Indian Ocean beach at dusk in the former pirate village of Eyl, in Somalia's semiautonomous northeastern state of Puntland, Somalia, March 6, 2017. Ben Curtis/AP hide caption
MOGADISHU, Somalia — Indian naval forces freed an Iranian fishing boat and its crew of 20 hijacked off Somalia after an operation lasting more than 48 hours, India's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The rescue of the Azini was completed Monday in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers (1,865 miles) from Mumbai, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said.
An official with the Puntland Maritime Police Force told The Associated Press that Indian forces disarmed 12 suspected Somali pirates, confiscated their mobile phones and released them. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.
The suspects and two Somali security guards later came ashore at Bandar Bayla in northeastern Somalia, the official said. Three of those who came ashore had minor injuries, but he did not specify whether they were suspects or guards, or how they were hurt.
India's ministry said the operation ended without casualties or injuries. It did not specify whether that account covered everyone aboard or only the rescued crew. It was unclear whether the crew remained on the vessel or were moved elsewhere.
The operation involved a warship, a maritime surveillance aircraft and marine commandos. An Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft airdropped additional commandos, the ministry said.
The Azini was hijacked Oct. 29 between Bandar Bayla and Hafun. A Puntland maritime police officer said on Sunday that it carried 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. The difference between that crew count and India's rescue figure could not immediately be explained.
Indian forces tracked the vessel by sea and air before securing it, the ministry said. It said there had been concern that pirates could use the boat as a floating base for attacks on commercial ships.
The Puntland official said regional authorities learned of the rescue only after it had taken place.
The hijacking followed a resurgence of Somali piracy across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. By August, pirates had hijacked six commercial vessels since April, some far from Somalia's coast. They included the oil products tanker Sibu 1, seized about 252 kilometers (136 nautical miles) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen.
In September, Puntland authorities said pirates killed five crew members of the tanker MT Honour 25 before security forces recovered it. The tanker had been held since April. Authorities said they detained 16 suspected pirates.
The renewed piracy adds to shipping risks in a region already disrupted by the Iran war. Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and threats by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi-linked shipping through Bab el-Mandeb have complicated oil transport routes.
Those disruptions have lengthened voyages and driven up tanker costs. Some oil shipments diverted around Africa face journeys up to a month longer.
International naval patrols and improved maritime security have sharply reduced Somali piracy over the past decade, but recent hijackings have renewed concerns about the threat.

articles.title_orig: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
articles.title_zh: Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries
articles.content_orig:
Investigations have begun in several European countries in response to the cyber-attacks
A spate of cyber-attacks that hit supermarket chains across at least 10 European countries on Monday has prompted European Union officials to warn of a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.
Supermarkets have reported problems in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany and Sweden, and the significant increase in freezer temperatures has forced retailers to discard food.
Temperatures in chains across Europe reportedly rose as high as 50C (122F).
No-one has yet admitted carrying out the cyber-attacks.
Supermarket chains said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared as high as 50C
The European Union has raised concerns about the attacks, which come three weeks after a cyber-attack disrupted as many as 700 French grocery stores, causing food losses estimated at tens of millions of euros.
The security of refrigeration systems as well as other devices that can be monitored remotely has heightened concerns about government-backed hybrid attacks.
The EU's food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the bloc was taking the incidents very seriously and warned of further disruption in the future.
Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier was careful not to attribute blame, but said: "These incidents of course show once again how cyber-attacks can disrupt essential services and affect citizens' daily lives."
"These are not isolated incidents and of course we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents."
In Italy , Giorgia Meloni's government called a meeting with intelligence chiefs, but said the impact was "currently very limited" and most of the food distribution chain had up-to-date security systems able to fend off such attacks.
At least four Co-op supermarkets in Sicily and one business in Tuscany were affected, according to the national cybersecurity agency.
Meloni's office said those businesses affected were "mostly still equipped with obsolete security systems, with interfaces directly exposed to the internet and inadequate authentication mechanisms".
Belgian supermarkets were among those hardest-hit, with dozens of stores reporting refrigeration failures. Federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.
UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers
Mathieu Tilman, a manager at a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, said he was shocked by this kind of attack: "I don't even understand how anyone could do this... How can we end up throwing away so much food? I find it truly distressing. In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."
In Ireland , 13 SuperValu stores were impacted by what the chain's owner, Musgrave Group, called a cyber-incident. "Replenishment of chilled and frozen ranges in the affected stores is well under way," a spokesman said on Monday.
A small number of corner shops in the Netherlands also suffered disruption. Last month, supermarket chain Albert Heijn had to take several services offline because of a separate cyber-attack.
There was disruption to refrigeration systems at the Rewe BÃ¼sken supermarket in western Germany after a cyber-attack on system provider Danfoss, the company told the BBC. Its systems have been back in operation since Monday afternoon.
In Portugal , the Mosqueteiros group said that incidents at seven IntermarchÃ© stores had been linked to a cyberattack, which "appears to have targeted an external service provider responsible for managing the refrigeration systems".
Swedish chain ICA also said "a limited number" of its stores had experienced refrigeration problems, without confirming a cyber-attack, and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
In Finland , irregular temperatures were detected in a few smaller grocery stores belonging to the Kesko group, which said it was investigating the issue.
In Estonia , at least one supermarket was attacked by hackers who raised the temperature in the refrigeration units to 50C, public broadcaster ERR reported.
Food losses are estimated in the tens of millions of euros
In the UK , the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has warned British retailers to update the software on fridge temperature controls.
The agency said the country was likely to suffer an AI-powered cyber-attack on critical national infrastructure within two years.
Richard Horne, the head of the National Cyber Security Centre, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there were a couple of instances in the UK where "vulnerable technology has been exploited" after the cyber-attacks.
"We don't know the full impact, but we do know there are a couple of instances where vulnerable technology has been exploited and we're working with those organisations."
Asked if there was any evidence that supermarkets in Britain or freezers of the same make or model had been targeted, Horne said: "It's not just supermarkets, it's through the whole food supply chain, and we've been working through the night alerting organisations where we can see they've got exposed technology that's vulnerable in this way."

articles.title_zh: UK will face AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure by 2028, official says
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The U.K. will likely face artificial intelligence cyberattacks on its critical infrastructure by 2028 as criminals and states, including China and Russia , increasingly use AI in their cyber activity, Britain 's cyber chief warned Tuesday.
That could include AI-powered malware for ransomware attacks as the technology will allow “vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long” to be discovered and exploited “at a scale that was once unimaginable,” Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center said.
In a speech marking the publication of the NCSC's annual cyber report, Horne said the leaders of businesses and organizations of all sizes who have "got away with tech on the cheap" will have to explain why “food isn't on the shelves, lights aren't on, businesses have gone under,” if they fail to invest in cybersecurity or update out-of-date technology.
Chinese cyber activity is the “most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the U.K.” while both Russia and China will routinely use AI to achieve their geopolitical goals, the report said. Russia is intentionally conducting cyber campaigns which fall below the threshold of armed conflict while Iran is carrying out attacks against the U.K. and targeting individuals who are a threat to the Iranian regime, Horne said.
The use of AI by states and criminals is highly likely to increase the scale and efficiency of hostile operations, but AI is more likely to be used to enhance and scale existing tactics and techniques rather than find brand new vulnerabilities, the report said.
Last week, governments and corporations worked on urgent security updates after the AI-assisted discovery of vulnerabilities in a programming language vital to 70% of websites globally. The two critical flaws identified by AI could allow bad actors to get unauthenticated access to sites which, in theory, could allow them to control a web server remotely without needing a password.
Technology “underpins the automation of physical processes that are vital to modern life,” Horne said. That includes, he said, electricity switching, sluice gates in water facilities, dam operations, manufacturing lines, heating and refrigeration controls. The recent cyberattacks on refrigeration systems in French supermarkets showed how easily hostile actors could exploit civilian infrastructure, Horne said.
Russia has already attacked critical infrastructure in Europe, according to the U.K. and EU member states that said Russia's FSB security service was behind an attack on Poland's energy grid in December 2025. If the attack had been successful, 500,000 people could have lost electricity during winter.
In the U.K., malicious cyber activity is costing organizations almost $20 billion every year, the NCSC said. In 2025, the carmaker Jaguar Land Rover suffered more than $260 million in direct losses following a cyberattack which also hit suppliers and dented the U.K. economy.
“We need every organization in the UK to take action now. Not only to protect their customers, services and livelihoods, but because cybersecurity is now part of the front line defense of our nation,” said Anne Keast-Butler, director of GCHQ, Britain’s signals intelligence agency, which the NCSC is part of.
That includes implementing basic but effective cybersecurity measures such as making sure devices are up to date, limiting administrator access to systems and backing up important files and data, the NCSC said.

articles.title_zh: Bonus PS Plus Premium Game Is Out Now for PS5
articles.content_orig:
You have got to wait another couple of weeks to gain access to the official set of new PS Plus Premium games for this month, but in the meantime, there's been a bonus addition to the service.
Not announced or highlighted by Sony or publisher Deep Silver, the new PS5 version of Metro Redux — which improves and enhances Metro 2033 and Metro: Last Light — has been added to PS Plus Premium. The old PS4 version was on there already, but now the listing has been updated to support the PS5 edition too.
This new PS5 version brings significant improvements over the original PS4 bundle of the two intense shooters, so they are worth revisiting again if you haven't already. Here's what to expect on PS5:
The third game in the series, Metro Exodus , was added to PS Plus Extra a few months ago, so now the entire franchise is playable natively on PS5 through Sony's subscription service. Now would also be a great time to catch up, with Metro 2039 out in February 2027.
Will you use PS Plus as a way to play through the Metro games for the first time, or do you fancy revisiting any of them? Let us know in the comments below.
[source store.playstation.com ]
Liam grew up with a PlayStation controller in his hands and a love for Metal Gear Solid. Nowadays, he's found playing the latest and greatest PS5 games as well as supporting Derby County. That last detail is his downfall.
That’s nice. Fantastic way to enjoy these titles.
I bought both of those games on PS4 so I snagged the free PS5 upgrades instead
I've never got round to playing any of the Metro games but I've heard great things. I don't do horror, how much do they lean into that or is it more of a focus on the story and world than straight-up scares?
Cool. Nice of them to double pack.
@springer17 I can't handle scares all that much and I never felt frightened of the series, mind you I've read the novels too and they are more terrifying because it relies on the readers imagination. Think of it more like how Fallout approaches it's combat/story beats. I'd call it more psychological and existential. For me the Horror was in the reality it's my city, for others I've talked to it's the claustrophobia. But the kind of scares that jump from Western studios isn't something you have to worry about. It's built differently is what I'm trying to say, I would call the games technical achievements even before those upgrades. You should definitely give them a try if you have the time.
I was actually thinking about playing these more recently so might finally be a good time to sign up for PS+ again for a month and knock them out.
@GirlVersusGame That's certainly enough to get me to at least give them a go, they've always intrigued me but I just never got around to trying them out. Thanks for the reply.
great games - paid full price for them back in the day - might go revisit them before the new one is out in Dec

articles.title_orig: Binance founder Changpeng Zhao addresses historic crypto hack: 'There's no 100% security'
articles.title_zh: Binance founder Changpeng Zhao addresses historic crypto hack: 'There's no 100% security'
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
It has been a busy few days for Changpeng Zhao in the wake of the hack on the enormous crypto platform he co-founded, Binance.
"It's been a pretty hectic process," Zhao, better known in crypto circles as CZ , told Yahoo Finance. "But the good thing is right now the withdrawals have been restored, the systems back to normal. People are free to use the platform without any issues now. And then all user funds are covered. The users did not suffer any loss."
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency trading platform and holds approximately $171 billion in total assets on its platform. The company is led by co-CEOs Richard Teng and Yi Le.
Hackers recently drained roughly $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from Binance on Oct. 29.
Here's what you need to know:
Blockchain intelligence firms and the FBI attributed the 20-minute raid with high confidence to TraderTraitor, an elite state-sponsored cyber unit tied to North Korea.
North Korea reportedly denied involvement.
Rather than cracking private cryptographic keys, the attackers reportedly breached internal automated transaction workflows via a Binance employee's laptop.
Read more: How to keep your crypto safe
Binance moved swiftly to stabilize the situation by guaranteeing full customer restitution, deploying corporate treasury reserves, Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) capital, and insurance funds to replenish user balances.
"There's no 100% security," CZ added. "So when you run a platform, especially a crypto platform the possibility is always there. I did not think it was going to be this big of magnitude, probably not."
